# Discrete and continuous number {#sec-discreteContinuous}

<!-- {{< include ../preamble.qmd >}} -->

::: {style="margin-top: 1em; font-size: 125%; font-weight: 1000; text-align: center;"}
To count or to measure.
:::

The title of this chapter should be natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ and real numbers $\mathbb{R}$. Everyone is familiar with these sets. Because the set of natural numbers is a subset of real numbers (e.g. 3 is also a real number), one can basically use real number and ignore the set of natural numbers.

So why such a title and why the distinction? The answer to the first question is because this book is about applied mathematics so there is more an emphasis about the properties of the numbers than nomenclature. In other words, natural numbers has the properties of discrete, while real numbers is a continuous set. The difference between discrete and continuous will appear in the statistics parts (discrete and continuous variables @sec-quantitativeVariable) and also implemented differently in coding (@sec-numeric)^[although interchangeble use is not fatal in R ].

## Formal {.unnumbered}
The formal definition is too technical^[requiring the field of topology] and will be omitted. Intuitively, in a discrete set, every number is isolated. In contrast, in a continuous set, any number has a neighbor no matter how small is the distance. That is why continuous numbers (real numbers) are represented by a continuous line, whereas natural numbers are represented by equidistant points.

## Examples {.unnumbered}
- Example of discrete numbers:
  - Even numbers: 2, 4, 6, 8,...
  - Odd numbers: 3, 5, 7, 9 ...
  - Prime numbers: 3, 5, 7, 11
  - And also the opposite (negative)

- Examples of continuous numbers that :
  - Fractions: $\frac{1}{3} = 0.3333\ldots, \frac{2}{4} = 0.5$
  - Irrational numbers^[when the patterns in the digits never repeats]
    - $\pi = 3.14\ldots$
    - $e = 2.71\ldots$
    - $\sqrt{2} = 1.41 \ldots$

## Tips and warnings {.unnumbered}
- Discrete number is mostly used for counting and indexing (e.g. in summation and product @sec-sum, for extracting element in a vector @sec-vector)
- Two ways of modeling evolution in time: in a difference equation (@sec-difference) time is moves in discrete time step, and and in differential equation (@sec-differential) time is continuous.
 - In probabilites^[anticipating future chapters], a sum ($\sum$)is used to compute the mean (and all other moments) if the variable is discrete, and integral ($\int$) is used if the variable is continuous

- Discrete numbers are mostly used for counting and indexing (e.g., in summation and product @sec-sum, or for extracting elements in a vector @sec-vector).

- Two ways of modeling evolution over time: in a difference equation (@sec-difference), time moves in discrete time steps; in a differential equation (@sec-differential), time is continuous.

- In probability^[Anticipating future chapters.], a sum ($\sum$) is used to compute the mean (and all other moments) if the variable is discrete, whereas an integral ($\int$) is used if the variable is continuous.


### Semantic/Terminology/Notation {.unnumbered}
- The discrete numbers are also called whole number, natural number or integer. The latter is the default term in coding.

- Discrete has nothing to do with "être discret".
